Anwar Sadat. On October 6, 1981, the Egyptian President was shot and killed by members of the militant Islamic group Egyptian Islamic Jihad during a military parade in Cairo.

The assassination occurred during a military parade celebrating the anniversary of the 1973 Yom Kippur War. The assassins fired from the reviewing stand, striking Sadat multiple times. He was pronounced dead within the hour. The attack also killed several senior military and government officials and wounded others in the stands.

Sadat's 1979 Camp David Accords with Israel, brokered by U.S. President Jimmy Carter, made him a pariah in much of the Arab world. Islamic militants opposed his secular, Western-aligned government and saw the peace with Israel as a betrayal of Arab and Islamic solidarity. Sadat had imprisoned thousands of Islamic activists and Coptic Christians in the months before his death as part of a crackdown on dissent. The assassins claimed to be defending Islam and Arab dignity against imperialism and Zionism.

Egyptian Islamic Jihad, the group behind the assassination, was later linked to Al-Qaeda. Hosni Mubarak, Sadat's vice president, succeeded him and ruled Egypt for thirty years, maintaining the Israeli peace and an authoritarian system.

Sadat's assassination marks a critical inflection point in Middle Eastern history: the moment when Islamic political opposition became violent and capable of striking at the highest levels of state power. Though Sadat had moved Egypt away from Soviet alignment toward the American sphere and toward peace with Israel—achievements of historic magnitude—he had also isolated himself politically by suppressing dissent and ignoring the rising power of Islamic sentiment. The assassination exposed the limits of imposed peace and revealed that a leader's personal security cannot be guaranteed if large segments of the population feel betrayed by his policies. The event demonstrated that Islamist militancy, not secular pan-Arabism, was becoming the dominant ideological force in the Middle East. It was a harbinger of the rise of modern militant Islamism throughout the region.
